root.note: Arabic ṣifr translates Sanskrit śūnya ‘empty’. The step from Medieval Latin zephirum to Venetian zero is the usual account.

history: The number zero is a borrowed idea as well as a borrowed word. Indian mathematicians had a symbol for ‘nothing’ and called it śūnya, ‘empty’. Arab scholars translated this as ṣifr. In 1202 the Italian mathematician Leonardo Fibonacci, who had learned the Indian numbers in North Africa, wrote the word in Latin as zephirum in his Liber abaci. The Venetian form was shortened to zero, and that is the word Italian uses today. A second Italian word comes from the same source: cifra, the ‘figure’ or digit. English has cipher, and French chiffre. In Italy temperatures and exam grades make zero common: ‘zero gradi’, ‘zero assoluto’.
historyEinfach: Zero comes from Arabic ṣifr, ‘empty’. The Arabs got the idea and the sign from India. An Italian mathematician, Fibonacci, brought it into Europe in 1202. Italian cifra (number, digit) and English cipher come from the same Arabic word.

elsewhere.text: English took zero from French or Italian in the 1600s. The older word cipher came earlier, straight from the Arabic through Medieval Latin.
